newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-CHANG AND MOYA LEAD BASELINE CHARGE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CHANG AND MOYA LEAD BASELINE CHARGE.

text.p: World number two Michael Chang and Spanish giant-killer Carlos Moya carried the flag for the baseline brigade on Wednesday when they charged into the third round of the Australian Open.
American Chang, the second seed and losing finalist to Boris Becker in Melbourne last year, wore down compatriot Richey Reneberg 6-3 7-5 6-1 in a relentlessly efficient display on Centre Court.
"I do not feel I am quite there," Chang said, before praising his opponent: "You definitely have to go out and beat him because he is not a player who will give it away."
Unseeded Moya, who succeeded where Chang failed last year by ousting sixth seed Becker on Monday, held his nerve after a poor start to beat American Patrick McEnroe 3-6 6-0 6-3 6-1.
Both Chang and Moya operated principally from the baseline, exploiting their speed around the court and consistent ground strokes to subdue their opponents.
Some of the harder hitters have complained that conditions at Melbourne Park this year are more favourable to baseliners than in past championships.

World number one Pete Sampras and Becker have complained about the softness of the tennis balls in use, claiming their slow speed through the air puts aggressive serve and volley players at a disadvantage.
Neither Chang nor Moya said they saw any difference in the balls from last year and the Spaniard suggested that Becker's tirade may have been sour grapes.

"I feel good about these balls. Maybe it is better for the baseliners (but) the one who complained was Becker -- maybe because he lost," said Moya, a tall, long-haired 20-year-old who has become a favourite with the female fans in Melbourne.

Becker's ousting has cleared a major obstacle in Chang's path to a possible final showdown with Sampras. Chang won his only grand slam, the French Open, as a 17-year-old in 1989 but now considers himself a much stronger, more mature player.

All five Spanish seeded players, their games developed on the slow clay courts of Europe, survived the first round, led by women's world number two Arantxa Sanchez Vicario and men's tenth seed Albert Costa.

After his first round win over Romanian qualifier Dinu Pescariu, Sampras said the balls were the softest he has ever experienced on tour and increased the risk of arm injuries because they had to be hit harder to generate the same speed.
Sixteenth seed Sabine Appelmans of Belgium became the first woman to advance to the third round with a 6-4 6-1 win over American Ann Grossman.
But men's 12th seed Magnus Gustafsson of Sweden lost out. Gustafsson, 30, was beaten 3-6 7-6 (8-6) 6-4 6-4 by 29-year-old German Karsten Braasch in a battle of the veterans.

Former champion Mary Pierce of France, now on a comeback, looked in superb form as she brushed past Natalia Medvedeva of Ukraine 6-2 6-2. Pierce ousted 13th seed Elena Likhovtseva of Russia in the first round.
